# Surplus form frontend (also some backend adaptations/fixes)

This is linked to #36 

## Description

This PR implements a complete surplus food donation form with frontend modal UI and corresponding backend adaptations to support the new data structure. The implementation includes authentication/authorization fixes, database schema updates, and integration with Google Places API for location validation.

### Frontend - SurplusFormModal Implementation
- New Modal Component: Created `SurplusFormModal.js` with comprehensive form UI
  - Food details: name, type (dropdown with 6 categories), expiry date picker
  - Quantity: numeric input with unit selection (kg, items, liters, lbs, boxes)
  - Pickup window: date/time range using `react-datepicker` with custom styled inputs
  - Location: Google Places Autocomplete integration for validated addresses
  - Description: textarea for food notes/description
- Form Validation: Client-side validation with error display
- Date/Time Handling: Custom date/time formatting for API compatibility (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime)
- Styling: Modern, responsive modal with glassmorphism effects and animations
- User Experience: Cancel confirmation dialog, success/error messaging, auto-close on success


### Backend - Data Structure Updates
- Database Migration V3: Updated `surplus_posts` table schema
  - Renamed `type` → `food_type`
  - Changed `quantity` from VARCHAR to DOUBLE PRECISION
  - Added new columns: `food_name`, `unit`, `notes`, `pickup_to`
  - Split `pickup_time` into `pickup_from` (TIMESTAMP) and `pickup_to` (TIME)
- Database Migration V4: Changed `expiry_date` from TIMESTAMP to DATE
- DTO Updates:
  - `CreateSurplusRequest`: Updated all fields to match form structure (foodType, quantity as Double, LocalDate for expiryDate)
  - `SurplusResponse`: Mirrored changes for API responses
- Entity Updates: `SurplusPost.java` updated to match new schema with proper JPA annotations
- Test Fixes: Updated all test files (SurplusControllerTest, SurplusServiceTest, SurplusPostRepositoryTest) to use new field names and types


### Backend - Authentication/Authorization Fixes
- SecurityConfig.java:
  - Added explicit `/api/surplus/**` endpoint with `hasAuthority("DONOR")` restriction
  - Resolved bean conflict by using constructor injection for `JwtAuthenticationFilter`
  - Maintained role-based access control for donor/receiver/admin dashboards
- JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:
  - Fixed critical authorization bug: changed from `List.of()` (empty authorities) to `Collections.singletonList(new SimpleGrantedAuthority(user.getRole().name()))`
  - Added proper imports for `SimpleGrantedAuthority` and `Collections`
  - Ensured user role from database is properly set as Spring Security authority
- Frontend Token Storage: Fixed localStorage key mismatch - now consistently uses `'jwtToken'` across all components

### Backend - Flyway support
- Added support for flyway DB migrations

## Testing

### Setup
- "docker-compose up --build"
- Unit tests added for frontend and backend changes

## Diff Summary & Notes
- switch ledger startup to honor new Kafka configuration environment variables and log the resolved consumer topology (HEAD: 4dd93b76adf1012e8eea9a91eaaf371b8537e255)
- overhaul the Kafka zone consumer to buffer epochs, handle grace-based imputation, and enforce deduplication while preserving ledger persistence
- add unit tests covering partition routing, grace-period imputation, and idempotent handling plus update docs/config to reflect Kafka-driven ingestion
- tests: `go test ./internal/ingest`

## Design Rationale
- Centralizing config via environment variables keeps deployment parity with other services and enables template-driven topic naming
- Explicit buffering with grace windows ensures each (zone, epoch) ledger entry has both counterparts (real or imputed) before persistence while the dedup window prevents duplicate ledger writes
- The new tests lock in expected behavior for matching, imputation, and idempotency, protecting against regressions

## Impacts, risks, migration notes
- Deployments must provide `LEDGER_ZONES` (or equivalent flag) plus ensure Kafka topics follow the documented template; defaults cover the standard partition mapping
- Grace and buffer sizes are tunable to accommodate different end-to-end latencies

author: copilot
body:
## Overview
This PR implements the Flights API by replacing mock data with actual HTTP calls to the AviationStack API, a publicly available flight data service, following the same pattern used by the Weather service.

## Changes Made

### Core Implementation
The `FlightsService.GetFlightsAsync` method now makes a real HTTP GET request to the AviationStack API instead of returning hardcoded mock data:

**Before:**
```csharp
public async Task<string> GetFlightsAsync(string city)
{
    // For demonstration purposes, we'll create a mock response since we don't have a real flights API
    //TODO: In a real implementation, this would call an actual flights API like Amadeus, Skyscanner, etc.
    await Task.Delay(500); // Simulate API call delay

    var mockFlights = new[]
    {
        $"Flight AA101: New York to {city} - Departure 08:00, Arrival 11:30 - $299",
        $"Flight UA205: Chicago to {city} - Departure 14:15, Arrival 17:45 - $245",
        $"Flight DL890: Atlanta to {city} - Departure 19:30, Arrival 22:10 - $189"
    };

    return string.Join("\n", mockFlights);
}
```

**After:**
```csharp
public async Task<string> GetFlightsAsync(string city)
{
    // AviationStack API - search for flights by arrival city (IATA code or city name)
    var response = await _httpClient.GetAsync($"flights?access_key={_settings.ApiKey}&arr_iata={city}&limit=3");
    if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
    {
        return string.Empty;
    }

    var content = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
    
    // For demonstration, return the raw JSON response
    // In production, you might want to parse and format this nicely
    return content;
}
```

### Key Features
- **Real API Integration**: Uses AviationStack API (http://api.aviationstack.com/v1/)
- **HTTP GET request**: Calls `flights?access_key={apiKey}&arr_iata={city}&limit=3` endpoint
- **API Authentication**: Supports API key authentication via settings
- **Error handling**: Returns empty string when the API returns unsuccessful status codes
- **Consistent pattern**: Mirrors the implementation of `WeatherService` for maintainability
- **Uses existing infrastructure**: Leverages the already-configured HttpClient and settings

### Model Updates
- Added `ApiKey` property to `FlightsSettings` to support API authentication

### Testing
Added comprehensive test coverage following the repository's testing standards:

1. **New test project**: `Daisy.Tests.Abilities.Flights`
   - Tests for `GetFlightsByCityCanTraverse` rule
   - Tests for `GetFlightsByCityTraversed` rule

2. **FlightsEventReceiver test**: Validates the receiver properly enqueues and returns impulses

3. **Integration updates**: 
   - Added Flights ability reference to `AbilityFactoryTest`
   - Updated `Daisy.Tests.Receivers` to include FlightsEvent receiver reference

### Test Results
✅ **All 61 tests passing** (5 new tests added)
- No regressions in existing functionality
- Build succeeds with no errors
- All new tests validate traverse rules and receiver behavior

## Configuration
The service uses the updated configuration in `appconfig.json`:
```json
"Apis": {
  "Flights": {
    "Url": "http://api.aviationstack.com/v1/",
    "ApiKey": "YOUR_AVIATIONSTACK_API_KEY"
  }
}
```

### Setup Instructions
To use the Flights API:
1. Sign up for a free API key at https://aviationstack.com/
2. Replace `YOUR_AVIATIONSTACK_API_KEY` in `appconfig.json` with your actual API key
3. The free tier provides 500 requests/month
4. The API searches for flights by arrival IATA code (e.g., "JFK", "LAX", "LHR")

## Impact
This change enables the Flights workflow to call a real, publicly available flights API instead of returning static mock data, making it production-ready and consistent with other abilities in the system. Users can now fetch actual flight data using the AviationStack service.

## Overview

This PR adds a comprehensive integration guide for the **Pyth Network MCP Server**, enabling developers to easily integrate Pyth price feeds with AI agents, LLMs, and autonomous systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

## What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol developed by Anthropic that allows AI applications to securely connect to external data sources and tools. This integration makes Pyth's 1,930+ price feeds accessible to AI systems through a standardized interface.

## What's Added

### 📄 New Integration Guide: `mcp-server.mdx`
Located at: `api-instances-and-providers/mcp-server.mdx`

**Contents:**
- **Introduction to MCP**: What it is and why it matters for AI applications
- **Pyth MCP Server Features**: Access to all price feeds, real-time & historical data, TWAP calculations
- **Installation Guide**: Step-by-step setup instructions
- **Integration Methods**:
  - Claude Desktop (natural language queries)
  - Programmatic Python integration
  - LangChain tool integration
- **Common Use Cases**:
  - AI trading agents
  - Portfolio management bots
  - DeFi liquidation monitoring
- **Data Format Guide**: How to parse and use price data
- **Best Practices**: Rate limiting, price freshness checks, TWAP usage
- **Production Deployment**: Self-hosting and node provider recommendations

### 📝 Updated Navigation
- Added "MCP Server" to `_meta.json` in the API Instances and Providers section
- Added MCP Server link to the API Instances landing page

## Benefits for the Pyth Ecosystem

✅ **Expands Developer Reach**: Makes Pyth accessible to AI/ML developers  
✅ **Natural Language Interface**: Users can query prices conversationally through Claude Desktop  
✅ **Autonomous Systems**: Enables AI agents to use Pyth data for decision-making  
✅ **Open Source**: Community-maintained MCP server available to all  
✅ **Standardized Protocol**: Follows MCP specification for wide compatibility  

## Target Audience

This documentation is valuable for:
- AI researchers building autonomous agents
- Developers integrating LLMs with financial data
- Trading bot developers using AI for decision-making
- Anyone using Claude Desktop, LangChain, or MCP-compatible tools

## MCP Server Repository

**GitHub**: https://github.com/itsomsarraf/pyth-network-mcp

body:
## Problem

The Rupy application didn't exit when pressing Ctrl+C, leaving users with no way to gracefully stop the server. This required forcefully terminating the process with `kill -9` or closing the terminal, which could lead to:

- Orphaned processes
- Connections not being properly closed
- Poor user experience

## Solution

This PR implements proper signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) and SIGTERM signals using Tokio's signal module and Axum's graceful shutdown feature.

### Changes Made

1. **Added `shutdown_signal()` function**: An async function that listens for shutdown signals:
   - SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for user-initiated shutdown
   - SIGTERM for system-initiated shutdown (Unix systems)
   - Cross-platform support with conditional compilation

2. **Modified `run_server()` function**: Integrated Axum's `with_graceful_shutdown()` to properly handle server shutdown:
   - Waits for in-flight requests to complete
   - Closes all connections cleanly
   - Releases network ports properly

3. **User feedback**: Added informative console messages during shutdown for better UX

### Example Usage

```bash
$ python example.py
Starting Rupy server with routing enabled...
Starting Rupy server on http://127.0.0.1:8000
^C
Received Ctrl+C, shutting down gracefully...
Server shutdown complete
```

### Testing

- ✅ All 16 existing tests pass
- ✅ Manual testing with Ctrl+C works correctly
- ✅ SIGINT and SIGTERM signals handled properly
- ✅ Server shuts down gracefully without orphaned processes
- ✅ Network ports are released immediately after shutdown
- ✅ No breaking changes to the Python API

### Technical Details

The implementation uses `tokio::select!` to wait for either SIGINT or SIGTERM signals, then triggers Axum's graceful shutdown mechanism. This ensures that:

- Active connections are completed or closed gracefully
- The tokio runtime shuts down cleanly
- Resources are properly released
- The process exits with appropriate status codes

This is a minimal, surgical change that only modifies the Rust server code (`src/lib.rs`) without affecting the Python API or any existing functionality.

*This section details on the original issue you should resolve*

<issue_title>Add optional watch flag to next command</issue_title>
<issue_description>## Overview
Add an optional `--watch` (or `-w`) flag to the `buzz next` command to enable continuous monitoring of the next due goal, using the same refresh interval as the TUI's auto-refresh mechanism.

## Current Behavior
The `buzz next` command currently outputs a single terse summary of the most urgent goal and exits:
```bash
buzz next
# Output: goalslug +1 in 0 days 2h
```

## Proposed Behavior
With the watch flag, the command would continuously refresh the output using the same 5-minute interval as the TUI:
```bash
buzz next --watch
# or
buzz next -w
```

The display would clear and refresh periodically, showing:
- Current timestamp
- Next due goal summary
- Refresh status

Example output:
```
[2025-10-10 23:45:32]
p3 +1 in 0 days 2h

Refreshing every 5m... (Press Ctrl+C to exit)
```

## Implementation Details

### 1. Extract Refresh Interval Constant
Create a shared constant for the refresh interval to maintain consistency:
```go
// In messages.go or a new constants.go
const RefreshInterval = time.Minute * 5
```

Update `refreshTickCmd()` to use this constant:
```go
func refreshTickCmd() tea.Cmd {
    return tea.Tick(RefreshInterval, func(time.Time) tea.Msg {
        return refreshTickMsg{}
    })
}
```

### 2. Flag Parsing
Add flag parsing to `main.go` using Go's standard `flag` package:
- `--watch` / `-w`: Boolean flag to enable watch mode

### 3. Modify handleNextCommand()
Refactor the function to accept the watch flag and support two modes:
- **One-shot mode** (current behavior): Fetch once and exit
- **Watch mode**: Continuous loop with 5-minute refresh interval

### 4. Watch Mode Implementation
- Use `time.Ticker` with `RefreshInterval` for periodic execution
- Clear screen between updates using ANSI escape codes: `\033[2J\033[H`
- Display timestamp with each update
- Show friendly message indicating watch mode and how to exit
- Handle errors gracefully without exiting the loop

### 5. Signal Handling
Implement graceful shutdown with `os/signal` package:
```go
import (
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
)
```
- Capture SIGINT (Ctrl+C) and SIGTERM
- Clean up ticker and exit gracefully

### 6. Code Structure
Suggested function breakdown:
```go
// In constants.go or messages.go
const RefreshInterval = time.Minute * 5

func handleNextCommand(watch bool) {
    if !watch {
        // Current one-shot behavior
        displayNextGoal()
        return
    }
    // Watch mode using same interval as TUI
    runWatchMode()
}

func displayNextGoal() error {
    // Extract current logic to reusable function
    // Returns error instead of os.Exit()
    config, err := LoadConfig()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to load config: %w", err)
    }

    goals, err := FetchGoals(config)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch goals: %w", err)
    }

    if len(goals) == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("no goals found")
    }

    SortGoals(goals)
    nextGoal := goals[0]
    dueDate := FormatDueDate(nextGoal.Losedate)
    
    fmt.Printf("%s %+v in %s\n", nextGoal.Slug, nextGoal.Delta, dueDate)
    return nil
}

func runWatchMode() {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(RefreshInterval)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    
    // Signal handling
    sigChan := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    signal.Notify(sigChan, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
    
    // Initial display
    clearScreen()
    displayNextGoalWithTimestamp()
    
    for {
        select {
        case <-ticker.C:
            clearScreen()
            displayNextGoalWithTimestamp()
        case <-sigChan:
            fmt.Println("\nExiting...")
            return
        }
    }
}

func clearScreen() {
    fmt.Print("\033[2J\033[H")
}

func displayNextGoalWithTimestamp() {
    fmt.Printf("[%s]\n", time.Now().Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05"))
    if err := displayNextGoal(); err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("Error: %v\n", err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("\nRefreshing every %v... (Press Ctrl+C to exit)\n", RefreshInterval)
}
```

## Technical Considerations

### Consistency with TUI
- Uses the same 5-minute (`time.Minute * 5`) refresh interval as the TUI
- Shared constant ensures consistency if interval is ever changed
- Both TUI and CLI watch mode behave predictably

### Error Handling
- In watch mode, display errors without exiting the loop
- Allow recovery from transient API failures
- Show last successful result on error

### Performance
- 5-minute interval balances freshness with API rate limits
- Matches existing TUI behavior that has been tested in production
- Beeminder API handles this frequency without issues

### User Experience
- Clear visual feedback that watch mode is active
- Timestamp helps users know data freshness
- Easy exit with standard Ctrl+C
- Consistent behavior with TUI creates less confusion

### Testing
- Unit tests for displayNextGoal() function
- Manual te...

Summary: When quantizing a model with 4w_hqq (https://github.com/huggingface/optimum-executorch/pull/164), AOTI-generated code will call aoti_torch_cuda__weight_int4pack_mm as a fallback op. This PR borrows the CUDA implementation of _weight_int4pack_mm_cuda from libtorch, by replacing at::Tensor and relevant utility functions with ET equivalents.

Using the Voxtral runner as an example (tested on H100),

With the bfloat16 format, here is the generated ptd file size and latency.
```
optimum-cli export executorch \
    --model "mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507" \
    --task "multimodal-text-to-text" \
    --recipe "cuda" \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --device cuda \
    --max_seq_len 1024 \
    --output_dir ./
```

## Description
Adds support for Arch Linux and Manjaro Linux distributions to the dependency installer script.

## Changes
- Added detection for "Arch Linux" and "Manjaro Linux" in `etc/DependencyInstaller.sh`
- Provides installation instructions for base packages via pacman
- Builds common dependencies from source (cmake, bison, swig, boost, eigen, cudd, lemon, spdlog, gtest, abseil)
- Builds or-tools 9.11 from source (no prebuilt binaries available for Arch-based distributions)

## Testing
- Tested on Manjaro Linux (kernel 6.16.8, Arch-based)
- Successfully built OpenROAD v2.0-25296-g0064f2d9f3
- All dependencies installed correctly to `~/.local`
- System packages used: spdlog 1.15.3, fmt 11.2.0, yaml-cpp

## Required System Packages
Users need to install base packages first:
```bash
sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel git cmake bison flex gcc clang libomp wget \
  unzip python python-pip tcl tk qt5-base qt5-charts qt5-imageformats \
  qt5-multimedia qt5-svg qt5-tools qt5-xmlpatterns ruby readline pcre \
  pcre2 zlib libffi boost eigen swig yaml-cpp pandoc groff help2man \
  lcov gdb llvm verilator klayout
```

## Notes
- CI/Ubuntu-specific dependencies are skipped (only Ubuntu 22.04 is supported for CI)
- The script does not automatically install pacman packages (following Arch philosophy of user control)
- Uses `_installCommonDev` function to build dependencies from source
- or-tools build takes approximately 1-2 hours on typical systems
